en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra entitled *Nairātmyaparipṛcchā*.
Then those non-Buddhist outsiders, possessing the view of apprehension, conceptualization, and discursive thought, approached the Mahāyānist and, with palms joined in respectful salutation, [spoke].
They asked a question concerning selflessness: "Noble son, it is taught by the Omniscient One that the body is selfless.
If the body is selfless, then a supreme self does not exist."
From what source do these—laughter, weeping, playfulness, anger, pride, envy, slander, and so forth—arise?
May the Blessed One dispel this doubt of ours: does the Supreme Self exist within the body, or does it not?
The Mahāyānists said: "O noble ones, it is said that the Supreme Self exists within the body;
it is certainly not that it does not exist."
In this matter, two things are not stated.
If it were said, "There is a supreme self," O friends, that would be false speech.

If it exists, O friends, how could it exist within this entire body—both internal and external—consisting of hair, nails, teeth, skin, body hair, veins, flesh, bones, fat, marrow, sinews, spleen, intestines, bowels, head, hands, feet, and limbs?
When investigated, the supreme self is not seen?
The non-Buddhists replied: "O son of good family, the supreme self is not seen;
we do not perceive it with the fleshly eye."
Sometimes those with the divine eye see it. The Mahāyānists say: "O worthy ones, even those with the divine eye do not see that which has no color, no form, and no conditioned formation."
How, then, is it seen? The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) ask: "Does it not exist?
The Mahāyānists reply: "O sirs, to say 'it does not exist' is false speech."
If it does not exist, how can these things—laughter, weeping, playfulness, anger, pride, envy, slander, and so forth—arise for it?
Therefore, one cannot say that it does not exist;
nor can both of these [existence and non-existence] be asserted.
The non-Buddhists said: "If, noble son, it is not said that 'it exists' or 'it does not exist,' then what can be the objective support here?
The Mahāyānists replied: "Friends, there is no objective support whatsoever."
The non-Buddhists asked: "Is it empty like space?
The Mahāyānists replied: "It is so, sirs; it is so.
It is empty like space."
The non-Buddhists said: "If it is so, noble son, then how are these things—laughter, weeping, play, anger, pride, envy, slander, and so forth—to be viewed?
The followers of the Mahāyāna replied: "They are to be viewed as being like a dream, an illusion, or a magical conjuration."
The non-Buddhists asked: "What is an illusion like? What is a dream like? And what is a magical conjuration like?"
The Mahāyānists say: "I have not grasped even a mere indication; a dream is a mere appearance whose nature is emptiness, and a magical illusion is a fabricated performance."
Thus, O worthy ones, all things are to be viewed as resembling a dream, an illusion, or a magical display.
Furthermore, two divisions are specified, namely: the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
Therein, what is called the conventional is this: "this is the self," this...

[As stated in the *Nirvāṇaparipṛcchā*, Vaidya p. 175: "The other [is as follows]: likewise, the notions of a living being (*jīva*), a person (*puruṣa*), an individual (*pudgala*), an agent (*kāraka*), and an experiencer (*vedaka*);
and whatever conceptualization there is of wealth, sons, wife, and so forth—"
That is what is called "conventional reality" (*saṃvṛti*):
wherein there is no self and no other,
and likewise no life-principle, no person, no spirit, no agent, no experiencer, and no wealth— this is the middle way regarding all phenomena.
In this regard, it is said:
Conventional reality and ultimate reality—these two divisions have been fully revealed.
Conventional reality is worldly phenomena; ultimate reality is supramundane. (1)
Sentient beings who have entered into conventional phenomena follow the power of the afflictions;
not knowing the ultimate truth, they wander for a long time in saṃsāra. // 2 //
Conventional reality is a worldly phenomenon, yet the unwise conceptualize it;
through their false conceptualization, they experience sufferings. // 3 //
Blind, foolish ordinary beings do not see the path to liberation;
they arise and cease incessantly within the five realms of existence. // 4 //
Enveloped by the worldly dharmas, the deluded wander like a wheel;
they do not know the ultimate truth wherein existence ceases.
Ensnared by the net of existence, they transmigrate again and again. (5)
Just as the moon and the sun come and go,
so too do beings in this world pass away from existence and return again.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, unstable, and momentary;
therefore, one who knows the ultimate truth should avoid the domain of conventional reality.
As for those gods, gandharvas, apsarases, and others who abide in the heavenly realm, there is falling away for all of them; all that is the fruit of conventional reality.
Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and Mahoragas—these too go again to hell; all that is the fruit of conventional reality (saṃvṛti).
Having attained the state of Śakra, the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin), and even the supreme station,
rebirth again in the animal realm— all that is the fruit of conventional reality (saṃvṛti).
Therefore, having renounced all this—divine and great bliss in heaven—the wise one should constantly cultivate the luminous bodhicitta. (11)
Lacking intrinsic nature, without support, entirely empty, and without abode, transcending all conceptual proliferation—this is the characteristic of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta). // 12 //
Neither hardness nor softness, neither heat nor cold, neither tactile sensation nor anything graspable—such is the characteristic of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta). 13.
Neither long nor short, neither round nor triangular, neither thin nor thick— such is the characteristic of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). (14)
Neither white nor red, neither black nor yellow; colorless and formless is the characteristic of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta). 15.
Unchanging, without appearance, without support, and without obstruction;
formless and resembling space—such is the characteristic of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta). // 16 //
Transcending all cultivation and beyond the sphere of the non-Buddhists, the form of the perfection of wisdom is the characteristic of the mind of awakening. // 17 //
Incomparable, without appearance, invisible, and indeed peaceful; pure by nature and without substance—such is the characteristic of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta). // 18 //
And all that is similar to it is essence-less, like a bubble; it is impermanent, selfless, and resembles an illusion or a mirage. // 19 //
Like a lump of clay fashioned into a jar, it is filled with manifold conceptual proliferation;
joined with passion, hatred, and the like, it is nothing but a dream or an illusion. // 20 //
Just as lightning within the clouds is not seen even for a moment, one should meditate on the supreme state through the vision of the perfection of wisdom. 21.
Playing, laughing, constant chatter, and likewise weeping;
dancing, singing, and instrumental music—all that is indeed like a dream. (22)
All conditioned phenomena of all embodied beings are like an illusion or a dream;
the dream is the mental construction of the mind, and the mind itself is like space. (23)
Whoever constantly meditates upon this method of the Perfection of Wisdom is liberated from all evils and attains the supreme state. // 24 //
This is that unsurpassed enlightenment proclaimed by all the Buddhas;
by practicing cultivation here, one attains the auspicious nirvāṇa. (25)
As many as are the faults of phenomenal existence (saṃvṛti), so many are the virtues of cessation (nirvṛti). Cessation is non-arising; it is not defiled by any faults. // 26 //
Then those non-Buddhists, being satisfied and free from conceptual construction, attained meditative absorption and became recipients of the sacrifice of the Mahāyāna.
The Inquiry into Selflessness in the Exposition of the Mahāyāna is completed.
